newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels, mediators set fresh Peru crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Rebels, mediators set fresh Peru crisis talks.

text.p: Mediators in Peru's 83-day hostage crisis planned to meet again on Monday with Marxist rebels holding 72 men at the Japanese ambassador's Lima home to try to restart stalled peace talks with the government.

Members of a three-man mediating commission met on Sunday with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) chief Nestor Cerpa but said afterward only that talks would continue on Monday. It was unclear if the government would take part.

"Our message today is that the discussions will continue tomorrow. In the next week, the discussions should be important ones," Canadian envoy Anthony Vincent, a mediator, said after the meeting inside the residence.

"We ask everyone involved to let these conversations continue in the way they have, seeking a solution that, although difficult, is viable," added Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, another member of the guarantors commission.
The mediators' visit gave the first sign that face-to-face talks could restart between the government and the rebels.

The local news media took their comments to mean negotiations would resume on Monday. State news agency Andina reported that rebels were willing to renew talks with the government Monday, but the report could not be confirmed.
The MRTA last week suspended talks aimed at reaching a solution to the nearly 12-week-old siege. It alleged the government planned to attack the residence through a tunnel.
President Alberto Fujimori has dodged questions about the tunnel and officials, including Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza, deny its existence.

But security sources told Reuters four tunnels were built in recent weeks while music was blasted from speakers around the mansion. Local newspapers published precise details about the tunnels, including maps describing their locations.

On Sunday, the scene outside the besieged mansion took on a carnival air, with hundreds of Fujimori supporters staging a noisy rally, shouting for the hostages' freedom and demanding the government concede nothing to the rebels. "Don't give in one inch; the people want peace!" they shouted.

Hostage sympathisers drove down a nearby street in a long line, tooting their horns in unison with the words "Long live peace" written on their windscreens. And street hawkers sold T-shirts saying "Just go home Nestor!!", a reference to Cerpa.

The MRTA, a Cuban-style group believed almost wiped out until it roared back to life Dec. 17 when it stormed the residence and seized hundreds of party guests, is demanding freedom for 458 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages.
Fujimori has rejected the demand but suggested he could make other concessions, flying to Cuba last week to arrange asylum for at least some of the rebels as part of a deal to end the crisis.

Fujimori and his allies have refused to rule out using force to free the hostages. "(The government) has to be prepared to act, using all instruments it considers necessary," Congressman Carlos Torres y Torres Lara, a Fujimori ally, said.

The hostages are held on two floors of the building with no electricity, limited water supplies, closed windows and no air conditioning amid one of Lima's hottest summers in memory. Twenty are in various stages of illness and doctors are occasionally let inside to treat the sick.

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer told local radio on Sunday that the hostages' health was generally good. But he called on the Red Cross to show greater "flexibility" so ministry doctors have easier access to the residence.
